target: 더블 룸을 예약했어요. 그런데 트윈 룸이에요.
english: I booked a double room, but it's a twin.
tip: Korean likes to pivot with a fresh sentence: 예약했어요 (yeyakhaesseoyo). 그런데 (geureonde)... – 'but' starts sentence two instead of folding into the middle of sentence one.

target: 방이 너무 추워요. 히터가 안 돼요.
english: The room is too cold. The heater doesn't work.
tip: 안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) stretches 되다 (doeda), 'become', into 'it doesn't work' – heaters, plans, phones, anything failing to function. One phrase covers most complaints.

english: Sorry, I misread the date.
tip: 잘못 (jalmot) in front of a verb means you did it wrong: 잘못 봤어요 (jalmot bwasseoyo) = 'saw it wrongly', i.e. misread. It works with almost any verb – hear, press, send.

english: I took a hundred photos at the beach.
tip: 장 (jang) counts flat things: 사진 백 장 (sajin baek jang) = 100 photos.

english: The wind was so strong my hat flew away.
tip: -어서 = so, because: 세서 (seseo) = because it was strong.

english: I sent Grandma a box of tangerines.
tip: 께 (kke) = honorific 'to': 할머니께 (halmeoni-kke) = to Grandma.

english: In Busan I tried raw fish for the first time.
tip: -어 봤어요 = have tried: 먹어 봤어요 (meogeo bwasseoyo) = tried eating.

english: It takes about three hours to Busan.
tip: 쯤 (jjeum) suffixes straight onto the amount: 세 시간쯤 (se sigan-jjeum) = about three hours. No separate 'about' word – the approximation rides on the number itself.

english: A round-trip ticket is more convenient than a one-way.
tip: 편도표보다 (pyeondopyo-boda), 'than a one-way ticket', can lead the whole sentence – 보다 (boda) marks the comparison wherever it sits, so the word order stays flexible.

english: We got lost once.
tip: 한 번 (han beon) = one time; written as one word, 한번 = 'just try it'.

english: A kind lady showed us the way.
tip: 가르치다 (gareuchida) isn't just classroom teaching – 길을 가르쳐 줬어요 (gireul gareuchyeo jwosseoyo) means she 'taught the road', i.e. showed the way. Directions are taught in Korean.

english: I left my sunglasses at the hotel.
tip: Korean narrates forgetting as two actions: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = 'put it down and came'. There's no single 'leave behind' verb – the sequence of events is the expression.

english: I made so many memories.
tip: Memories arise on their own in Korean – 생겼어요 (saenggyeosseoyo), from 생기다 (saenggida), means they 'came into being'. You don't make 추억 (chueok), memories; they happen to you.

english: After my business trip I traveled two more days.
tip: Korean counts days with native words of their own: 이틀 (iteul) = two days, 하루 (haru) = one day – not number + 'day'. So 이틀 더 (iteul deo) = two more days, no counter needed.

english: You should definitely go to Busan.
tip: 가 보세요 (ga boseyo) is 'try going' – the -어 보세요 (-eo boseyo) ending turns a command into a friendly 'give it a try', much softer than a bare 'go'.

target: 이 여행 앱을 한번 써 보세요.
english: Give this travel app a try.
tip: 써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try using it. 쓰다 (sseuda) is one verb for both 'write' and 'use' – context decides which; here it's using the app.

english: I pack my passport first.
tip: -부터 (-buteo) means 'starting with' – not just for times. 여권부터 (yeogwon-buteo) = 'starting with the passport', i.e. the passport comes first.

english: I packed a swimsuit and a hat.
tip: 하고 (hago) is 'and' for nouns only: 수영복하고 모자 (suyeongbok-hago moja) = swimsuit and hat. It can't join sentences – that takes a verb ending.

english: I only took half my clothes.
tip: 만 (man) = only: 반만 (ban-man) = only half.

english: I've already made plans for the next trip.
tip: You stand a plan up in Korean: 계획을 세웠어요 (gyehoegeul sewosseoyo) uses 세우다 (se-uda), 'to stand something up' – buildings and plans take the same verb.

english: This time I'm going to try Gyeongju.
tip: -어 볼 거예요 = will give it a try: 가 볼 거예요 (ga bol geoyeyo) = will try going.

english: I want to work at a good company.
tip: -고 싶어요 = want to: 다니고 싶어요 (danigo sipeoyo) = want to work there.

english: I passed the document screening.
tip: 붙다 (butda) literally means 'stick': 서류 전형에 붙었어요 (seoryu jeonhyeong-e buteosseoyo) = you stuck to the screening, so you passed.

english: Sadly, I got cut at the document stage.
tip: 떨어지다 (tteoreojida) is literally 'fall': 서류에서 떨어졌어요 (seoryu-eseo tteoreojyeosseoyo) = fell off at the document stage. Failing is falling.

english: I'm preparing hard for the interview.
tip: -고 있어요 = am -ing: 하고 있어요 (hago isseoyo) = am doing it.

english: I'm so nervous because of the interview.
tip: 긴장돼요 (ginjang-dwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda) 'become' – nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not something you are.

english: I got a call from that company.
tip: 연락이 오다 (yeollagi oda) = to get a call/message (lit. contact comes).

english: The manager kindly explained it to me.
tip: 설명해 주셨어요 (seolmyeonghae jusyeosseoyo) adds 주다 (juda) 'give' to the verb – the explaining was done FOR you, as a favor. Without it, they just explained.

english: The manager began the meeting.
tip: 부장님이 (bujangnim-i) is someone you honor, so the verb takes -(으)시- (-si-) inside: 시작하셨어요 (sijakhasyeosseoyo), not plain 시작했어요 (sijakaesseoyo).

english: My coworkers are all kind.
tip: -들 (-deul) marks a plural: 동료들 (dongnyodeul) = coworkers. Korean often leaves plurals unmarked – you add it when the many-ness matters.
